text: I love it when people take mandatory word and say, ah, they really don't mean what they mean. A table is not a table, even though it's a table. So they said it's directory. And you're saying, if I remember right, you were talking about that with regard to directory as it relates to dismissing the proceeding. It's a directory, so you can't really dismiss. Is that what those cases are talking about?

speaker: jeffreyford
text: The cases talk about both the mandatory and jurisdictional requirement there that a violation of 53.05 does not lead to dismissal.

speaker: brianquinn
text: OK, dismissal because you don't lose your jurisdiction, basically.

speaker: jeffreyford
text: Yes, yes, your honor. That would be the only remedy.

speaker: brianquinn
text: OK, is that related? Is the directory language related to not losing your jurisdiction and being able to dismiss? Or does it have other meaning with regard to, hey, you've got to eventually try these matters or hear these matters. You say shall, what's the remedy? Are you saying there's no remedy? You can take a shall and delay forever?

speaker: jeffreyford
text: I'm certainly not saying that delay can be done forever. Justice Dawson noted during Post and Counsel's argument that sufficiency has not been raised on appeal here. But just because sufficiency has not been raised here, it was raised at the lower court level there. Because there has to be every 10 working days, there has to be another continuing detention hearing to determine whether the factors are still present there. So there isn't really any question that delay can go on indefinitely there. Just a matter of what is the remedy for violation 53.05b and the 10-day requirement there. And the answer is there is no remedy for a violation that 10 working day rule. And the reason for that is because the legislature intended the statute to be directory in order to further the purpose of Title III, which is protecting the rights of juveniles and ensuring public safety and welfare. Given the nature of the offenses here, appellant has been charged with the offenses of murder and aggravated robbery there. Given the nature of the offenses and in order to protect the interests of both society and appellant, his detention serves a legitimate regulatory purpose, which is compatible with the fundamental fairness demanded by the Due Process Clause in juvenile proceedings.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Does a juvenile have a right to presumption of innocence? Yes, Your Honor. Absolutely.

speaker: judyparker
text: Is it a violation of a defendant's due process rights if the defendant were an adult, incarcerated, pending trial without bail, based solely on the crime that the defendant was alleged to have committed?

speaker: jeffreyford
text: Your Honor, I'm not sure whether it says, article says 1715 of Code Criminal Seizure governs adult confinement there. And it's a multifactored approach, one of which, of course, is the interest of society there. And so you would have to consider a multifaceted approach, but certainly the protection of society is a valid consideration in adult confinement.

speaker: judyparker
text: Well, at what point in time does holding this child without an adjudication hearing become a due process violation?

speaker: jeffreyford
text: Your Honor, I don't have an answer for that. There's nothing, no case I've been able to find, giving a set time period for when pre-trial incarceration for juvenile becomes a due process violation.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Have you, in effect, had a de facto adjudication hearing here every time you had that 10-day hearing, and the court says you're a threat to society because you're a murderer?

speaker: jeffreyford
text: No, no, Your Honor. Certainly there has been no finding of guilt in here. This is the 10-day requirement. It's only for purposes of continued pre-trial detention.

speaker: brianquinn
text: But in effect, they're saying you've been charged with murder, and boy, that's bad. And so we're going to keep you locked up for some more. Isn't that kind of a quasi-adjudication, if it continues forever, which you said it could?

speaker: jeffreyford
text: Well, Your Honor, it's certainly no different than an adult who is incarcerated for a year or two. There's no finding of guilt, even if the adult continues to be confined for a lengthy period of time. Likewise, there has been no adjudication hearing here just because the appellant has been incarcerated for over a year.

speaker: judyparker
text: So the adult would have the benefit of the Speedy Trial Act, which, in essence, is what the Family Code Section 53.05 embodies. It gives a short or a 10-day time limit, and understanding that that limit can be longer, for example, for a psychological evaluation, if there's going to be a certification as an adult. And there are cases, and I believe you cite them in your brief, that deals with those situations. I couldn't find a case that dealt with the due process argument. If the child's not certified, how long is too long to hold without having the adjudication hearing? Because under Subsection A of the statute, under 53.05, the burden is on the judge to set the hearing. And certainly, the judge in this case would have had notice when the habeas corpus proceeding was going on, and at that time, the child had been held for 86 days.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Mr. Ford, we're going to let you answer that question. I know the time's expired, and unless the judges have other questions, we'll let you answer this one, and then we'll flip on over to Ms. McMillan and her rebuttal.

speaker: jeffreyford
text: Okay. Yes, sir. Justice Parker, there's no specific time period before which a pretrial incarceration becomes oppressive there. That's only been the case for the last year.

speaker: larrydoss
text: Excuse me, Your Honor? That's only been the case for the last year that nothing has occurred.

speaker: jeffreyford
text: No, nothing has occurred that's in the record. That doesn't mean that pretrial hearings haven't been happening or will be happening in the future here. Pretty soon is my understanding outside the record.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Thank you, Mr. Ford. Thank you. Any other questions of Mr. Ford of the state? And Mr. Ford, I wanted to say that you're a good sport for allowing us to continue to ask questions. speaker: lornamcmillio
text: Two points on rebuttal. And first, outside the record, I have had no notification at all that pretrial hearings will be proceeding soon. And the state responded that the default is that she is acting as a magistrate. But Your Honors, default is not the standard for constitutional due process. The state's argument is essentially, we do this because this is the way we've always done it. But the most recent order of the Board of Judges from Lubbock County specifically appoints and refers cases to Judge McNamara as an associate judge for juvenile matters. This is what the Board of Judges authorized her to do. And while under her appointment as an associate judge or even a magistrate judge, those orders can limit her powers, they cannot expand them. So even her order of referral under the magistrate status does not expand her powers under 54.78 of the government codes to include the power to detain juveniles. It is not enumerated there.

speaker: judyparker
text: Well, the Board of Judges has a responsibility of reappointing the associate judges, I believe it's every four years. As a matter of course, there's nothing in the order itself that says, for example, that the order would expire.

speaker: lornamcmillio
text: That's correct, Your Honor. And I don't believe it did expire, but I believe it was substituted, although it doesn't say it in name, by the very specific order appointing her as a judge for juvenile matters and then referring those juvenile matters to her after the statute was amended and House Bill 79 was passed in 2011.

speaker: judyparker
text: But none of those statutes work together though. There would be some responsibilities and powers as the associate judge for juvenile matters, hearing a final adjudication, for example, that Judge McIntyre would not have as the Lubbock County magistrate. speaker: lornamcmillio
text: They could potentially work together if jurisdiction for a magistrate to proceed outside of chapter four of the juvenile code was authorized, but they're bound by those jurisdictional limits of 54.01. And a magistrate can only proceed unless that juvenile court judge is otherwise unavailable. As the state stated, he wasn't otherwise unavailable.

speaker: judyparker
text: No, that's for a referee, I believe.

speaker: lornamcmillio
text: Oh, no, Your Honor. The referee was under subsection, I believe, G, but the magistrate is under subsection G. Referee is the one just right after that. The referee is appointed and the referee can proceed over all matters of the course, so long as those cases are referred to them under that appointment status. Your Honor, Second Chief Justice Quinn, my second point, you asked if the statute says shall, and it does. And yes, there are some cases, none controlling at this point for this jurisdiction, whether that's mandatory or directory in nature. And yes, the burden is on the court to hold that hearing. There is some instructive case law from Texarkana in the matter of SD, which was cited in my brief, that the delay was only justified where the trial court could not conduct a diagnostic study that was mandatory. So basically that adult certification, which you referenced, Justice Parker, when certification as an adult isn't an issue when the investigation has been closed, they're really, the burden has been on the state and the judge to say, all right, we have to have this trial. We have to adjudicate. You're out of excuses. And I guess maybe mandamus relief is the juveniles. Maybe after that, I'm not sure.

speaker: larrydoss
text: Let me ask you a question along those lines. Suppose Mr. Ford is correct and the state does decide to have an adjudication hearing on month 16 after your client's been held. Does that meet your second issue?

speaker: lornamcmillio
text: No, Your Honor, it doesn't because he's still been violated. He's had constitutional due process issues this whole entire time. And Schultz says Martin goes.

text: What would the relief, what would the remedy be if there's a finding at that adjudication hearing that your client should continue to be held?

speaker: lornamcmillio
text: I think you would look to whether the defendant was irreparably harmed by how long it took that case to get to trial and the irreparable harm and fundamental harm that he suffered while he was in detention, not being treated as a juvenile is supposed to be treated, not being afforded constitutional due process while evidence sits around and we wait for fact finders to come and testify at trial. This could go on indefinitely, Your Honors.

speaker: brianquinn
text: It sounds a little bit like considerations regarding or underlying speedy trial. The loss of evidence and sitting in jail and all that.

speaker: lornamcmillio
text: And I believe that that's probably the analysis that we should apply in this context to juveniles. What are the standards of a violation of due process for violating the speedy trial right? He was not near the offense when it happened and that's all on the record. And so we do need a way for this to be brought to trial.
